        Next, let $\underline{d}\in \Sigma(C)$. Let $Z\subseteq C$ be a subcurve. 
         By Equation \eqref{eq:dZ-stable} we have $d_{F^Z_i} > g_{F^Z_i} - 1$ for every $i=1,\dots,t_Z$,  hence $d_{Z^c}\geq \sum_{1\le i\le t_Z}  g_{F^Z_i}$. Thus
        \[
        d_Z\leq g - 1 - \sum_{1\le i\le t_Z} g_{F^Z_i} = g_Z + \delta_Z - t_Z -1 = N_{\varphi(Z)},
        \]
        where we use Equation \eqref{eq:gZ} in the first equality and (i) in the second, proving (iii). 
        
        Finally, let $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ be a strong orientation of $\Gamma_C$ such that $\underline{d}_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}=\underline{d}\in \Sigma(C)$.  Let $Z$ be an honest hyperelliptic subcurve  of $C$.  Let $V_Z \subseteq V(\Gamma_C)$ be the set of vertices corresponding to the irreducible components of $Z$. Thus $|V_Z| \leq 2$ and $|V_Z|=2$ if and only if $Z$ is an honest hyperelliptic pair.  By Proposition~\ref{prop:catanese_hh} (iv) every connected component $Z'$ of $Z^c$ intersects $Z$ in exactly two nodes. Since $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ is strong, that means that the edges corresponding to these two nodes must be one oriented towards $Z$ and the other to $Z^c$. That means that exactly half the edges in $E(Z, Z^c)$ must be oriented towards $Z$. Recall Equation \eqref{eq:another-strong} and the definition of $\tau'$  above it. We have that $\tau_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}, V_Z}' = t_Z= \frac{\delta_Z}{2}$, and hence
        \[
        d_{Z} = d_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}, V_Z} = g_Z - 1 +\frac{\delta_Z}{2} = \frac{k_Z}{2}.
        \]
    
       Moreover, again by Proposition~\ref{prop:catanese_hh} (iv), we have $\delta_Z=2t_Z$, hence, by using (i), we obtain $N_{\varphi(Z)}=g_Z-1+\frac{\delta_Z}{2}$. Finally, we have to check that $1\le d_Z<k_Z$. If $Z=C$, then $d_C=g-1$ and $k_C=2g-2$, hence clearly $1\le d_C<k_C$. So assume $Z\ne C$, hence $\delta_Z$ is positive, and it is also even since $\delta_Z=2t_Z$. Since $C$ is stable, we see that $2g_Z-2+\delta_Z$ is positive and even, so 
        $d_Z=g_Z-1+\frac{\delta_Z}{2}\geq1$, from which we also get $d_Z<2g_Z-2+\delta_Z=k_Z$. This concludes the proof of (iv).
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
Let $\Gamma$ be a graph. An orientation ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}$ on $\Gamma$ is \emph{quasi-Eulerian} if $|\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)|\le 1$, for every $v\in V(\Gamma)$.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def: qe}
    A multidegree $\underline{d}$ on $\Gamma$ is \emph{quasi-Eulerian} (respectively \emph{Eulerian}) if $\underline{d}=\underline{d}_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}$ for some quasi-Eulerian (respectively Eulerian) orientation ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}$ on $\Gamma$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
Let $\Gamma$ be a graph. An \emph{ear-decomposition} of $\Gamma$ is a sequence of subgraphs $(\Gamma_1, \dots,\Gamma_n)$ such that $\Gamma=\cup_{1\le i\le n} \Gamma_i$, where $\Gamma_1$ is an isolated vertex and $\Gamma_j$ is a $\left(\cup_{1\le i\le j-1}\Gamma_i\right)$-ear for every $j=2,\dots,n$. We denote by $v_i$ and $w_i$ the (possibly coinciding) end-vertices of $\Gamma_i$.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:balanced-prescribed-edge}
Let $\Gamma$ be a graph, and let $h\in E(\Gamma)$. Fix an orientation on
$h$. Then there exists a quasi-Eulerian orientation $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ on $\Gamma$ extending the 
orientation of $h$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
It is enough to argue on each connected component of $\Gamma$. Let $\Gamma_0$ be
a connected component.

Pair the odd-valent vertices of $\Gamma_0$
and connect the two vertices of each pair with one temporary additional edge. The resulting connected graph
$\Gamma_0^+$ is Eulerian. Choose an Eulerian orientation $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}^+$ of $\Gamma_0^+$
starting by traversing $h$ in the prescribed direction if $h\in E(\Gamma_0)$. 
Orient the non-temporary edges of $\Gamma_0$ according to $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}^+$, and then
discard the temporary edges. In $\Gamma_0^+$ every vertex $v$ has $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}^+}(v)=0$, and
it is incident to at most one temporary edge. Hence
deleting the temporary edges gives rise to an orientation $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ on $\Gamma$ such that  $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)$ differs from $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}^+}(v)$ at each vertex $v$ by $0$, $1$, or
$-1$. Therefore, $|\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)|\leq 1$ for every $v\in V(\Gamma_0)$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:strong-qE}
    Let $\Gamma$ be a $2$-edge connected graph. Let ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}$ be an orientation on $\Gamma$. Assume that $(\Gamma_1,\dots,\Gamma_n)$ is an ear decomposition of $\Gamma$ such that ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}|_{\Gamma_i}$ is a quasi-Eulerian orientation on $\Gamma_i$ for $i=1,\dots,n$. Then ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}$ is strong.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
We proceed by induction on $n$. If $n=1$ then $\Gamma$ is an isolated vertex and we have nothing to prove. If $n=2$, then $\Gamma$ is a cycle. Any quasi-Eulerian orientation on a cycle has
$\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=0$ for every $v\in V(\Gamma)$, hence it is Eulerian and strong.
    
    Let $n\ge3$. Set $\Gamma'=\cup_{1\le i\le n-1} \Gamma_i$ and ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}':={\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}|_{\Gamma'}$. We let $u_n$ and $z_n$ be the (possibly coinciding) vertices of $\Gamma_n$ such that $u_n,z_n\in V(\Gamma')$. Assume, without loss of generality, that $u_n=\sigma_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(e)$ for some $e\in E(\Gamma_n)$.  
    Notice that $(\Gamma_1,\dots,\Gamma_{n-1})$ is an ear decomposition of $\Gamma'$. Since ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}'|_{\Gamma_i}={\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}|_{\Gamma_i}$ is quasi-Eulerian for every $i=1,\dots, n-1$, by induction, the orientation ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}'$  on $\Gamma'$ is strong. In particular, every vertex in $V(\Gamma')$ is strongly $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$-connected to $u_n$ and $z_n$.

    Consider $v\in V(\Gamma)\setminus V(\Gamma')$. It is clear that  $u_n$ is ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}|_{\Gamma_n}$-connected to $v$, hence $u_n$ is ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}$-connected to $v$. Similarly, $v$ is ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}$-connected to $z_n$. On the other hand, $z_n$ is ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}$-connected to $u_n$. Hence $v$ is ${\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}$-connected to $u_n$ and we have proven that $v$ is strongly $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$-connected to $u_n$. This shows that every vertex in $V(\Gamma)$ is strongly $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$-connected to $u_n$, which shows that the orientation $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ is strong.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:comp-orient}
Let $\Gamma$ be a connected graph with no separating edges, and let
$a,b\in V(\Gamma)$. Then there exists a strong orientation $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}_\Gamma$ of
$\Gamma$ with the following property. Let $\widehat{\Gamma}$ be obtained from
$\Gamma$ by adding one auxiliary edge $f$ connecting $a$ and $b$. If
$\widehat{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}_\Gamma$ is the orientation of $\widehat{\Gamma}$ extending
$\operatorname{\mathfrak o}_\Gamma$ by orienting $f$ from $a$ to $b$, then $\widehat{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}_\Gamma$ is
quasi-Eulerian.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
If $\Gamma$ has $1$ vertex, the statement is immediate. Assume then that $\Gamma$ has at least $2$ vertices. Since $\Gamma$ has no
separating edges, it is $2$-edge connected, so there is an ear decomposition
$(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_n)$ of $\Gamma$. Thus
$\Gamma_1$ is the initial isolated vertex, and $\Gamma_j$ is an ear for every
$j\geq 2$.

We define an auxiliary graph $G$ as follows. Its
vertex set is $V(\Gamma)$, and for every $j\geq 2$ it has one edge $h_j$ joining
the two (possibly coinciding) end-vertices  of the ear $\Gamma_j$. The initial isolated vertex $\Gamma_1$ contributes no edge.

Add to $G$ one auxiliary edge $h$ from $a$ to $b$, and denote
the resulting graph by $\widehat{G}$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:balanced-prescribed-edge}, there exists a quasi-Eulerian orientation
$\widehat{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}$ of $\widehat{G}$ such that $h$ is oriented
from $a$ to $b$. 

Replace each oriented edge $h_j$ by the corresponding ear $\Gamma_j$, oriented consistently if its end-vertices are distinct and cyclically otherwise. The resulting orientation $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}_\Gamma$ is strong by Lemma~\ref{lem:strong-qE}. Replacing each $h_j$ by $\Gamma_j$, and $h$ by $f$, preserves at every vertex the difference between the numbers of incoming and outgoing edges. Thus $\Delta_{\widehat{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}_\Gamma}(v)=\Delta_{\widehat{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}}(v)$ for every $v\in V(\Gamma)$, so $\widehat{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}_\Gamma$ is quasi-Eulerian.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:q_orient}
Let $\Gamma$ be a stable $2$-edge connected graph. For every $\operatorname{C_1}$-set
$S\subseteq E(\Gamma)$, there is an orientation $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ on $\Gamma$ with
associated multidegree $\underline{d}$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ is strong and quasi-Eulerian;
\item[(ii)] for every $e\in S$, if $v=\sigma_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(e)$, then $d_v\leq k_v-1$;
\item[(iii)] for every $e\in S$, if $w=\tau_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(e)$, then $d_w\geq 1$;
\item[(iv)] if $\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_k$ are the connected components of
$\Gamma\setminus S$, then $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}|_{\Gamma_i}$ is strong for every $i$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Let $\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_k$ be the connected components of
$\Gamma\setminus S$. Since $S$ is a $\operatorname{C_1}$-set,
$\Gamma/(E(\Gamma)\setminus S)$
is a cycle, and $\Gamma\setminus S$ has no separating edges. In particular, each $\Gamma_i$ has no separating edges.

The vertices of the quotient graph $\Gamma/(E(\Gamma)\setminus S)$ correspond to
the connected components $\Gamma_i$, and its edges are the elements of $S$ (see Figure \ref{fig:C_1-set}). Since
this quotient is a cycle, we may label the components and the edges of $S$
cyclically as
\(
S=\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\},
\)
so that $e_i$ joins $\Gamma_i$ to $\Gamma_{i+1}$, using indices modulo $k$ (so 
$\Gamma_{k+1}=\Gamma_1$ and $e_{0}=e_k$). In the case $k=1$, this means that the quotient cycle
has one vertex and one loop; in this case, the edge $e_1$ may be either a loop in $\Gamma$ or a
non-loop edge whose endpoints lie in the same component of $\Gamma\setminus S$.

Orient each $e_i$ from $\Gamma_i$ to $\Gamma_{i+1}$ (when $k=1$ and $e_1$ is a non-loop edge, choose either orientation for $e_1$), and let $v_i\in V(\Gamma_i)$ and $w_{i+1}\in V(\Gamma_{i+1})$ be the source and target of $e_i$.  

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:comp-orient} to $\Gamma_i$
with $a=v_i$ and $b=w_i$. We obtain a strong orientation $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}_i$ of $\Gamma_i$
such that, after adding an auxiliary edge
$f_i$ oriented from $v_i$ to $w_i$,
the extended orientation $\widehat{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}_i$ of $\widehat{\Gamma}_i$ (notation as in Lemma~\ref{lem:comp-orient}) is
quasi-Eulerian. Define $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ on $\Gamma$ by setting $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}|_{\Gamma_i}=\operatorname{\mathfrak o}_i$, and by
keeping the cyclic orientation of the edges $e_1,\ldots,e_k$.

For every $x\in V(\Gamma_i)$, the contribution to $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(x)$ from the two
$S$-incidences of the quotient at $\Gamma_i$, namely $e_{i-1}$ and $e_i$ counted
cyclically and with multiplicity, is exactly the contribution of the auxiliary edge
$f_i$ oriented from $v_i$ to $w_i$. Hence $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(x)=\Delta_{\widehat{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}_i}(x)
\text{ for every } x\in V(\Gamma_i).$

Since each $\widehat{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}_i$ is quasi-Eulerian, $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ is quasi-Eulerian. Moreover,
each $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}_i$ is strong, and the edges $e_1,\ldots,e_k$ orient the quotient
$\Gamma/(E(\Gamma)\setminus S)$ as a directed cycle. It follows that $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ is
strong on $\Gamma$. This proves (i) and (iv). 

It remains to prove (ii) and (iii). Recall that $d_x=g_x-1+\tau'_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},x}$ and
$k_x=2g_x-2+\delta_x$ for every $x\in V(\Gamma)$. Since $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ is quasi-Eulerian and
$\tau'_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},x}+\sigma'_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},x}=\delta_x$, we have
$\lfloor \delta_x/2\rfloor \le \tau'_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},x}\le \lceil \delta_x/2\rceil$.

First suppose that  $e\in S$ is a loop at $v$. Then $S=\{e\}$. Loops contribute neither
to $\delta_v$ nor to $\tau'_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},v}$. If $\delta_v=0$ (the graph with $1$ vertex), stability gives $g_v\ge 2$, hence
\[1\le d_v=g_v-1\le 2g_v-3=k_v-1.\] If $\delta_v>0$, then $\delta_v\ge 2$ because
$\Gamma$ has no separating edges, and $g_v\ge 1$ because $e$ is a loop at $v$. Thus \[1\le g_v-1+\lfloor\delta_v/2\rfloor\le d_v\le
g_v-1+\lceil\delta_v/2\rceil\le 2g_v-3+\delta_v=k_v-1\]
(the first and the last inequality use $g_v\ge 1$ and $\delta_v\ge 2$). Hence  (ii) and (iii) hold when $e$ is a loop.



Now let $e_i\in S$ be an edge that is  not a loop. Write $v_i=\sigma_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(e_i)\in V(\Gamma_i)$ and
$w_i=\tau_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(e_{i-1})\in V(\Gamma_i)$. Since $\Gamma_i$ has no separating edges, if
$v_i=w_i$, then either $\delta_{v_i}=2$ or $\delta_{v_i}\ge 4$; while if $v_i\neq w_i$,
then $\delta_{v_i}\ge3$ and $\delta_{w_i}\ge 3$. Also, if $x\in\{v_i,w_i\}$ and $\delta_x=3$,
then the two internal incidences of $x$ inside $\Gamma_i$ cannot be oriented in the same
direction, because $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}|_{\Gamma_i}$ is strong. Thus exactly one of them enters $x$.

We now prove (ii). Let $v=v_i=\sigma_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(e_i)$.

If $v_i=w_i$ and $\delta_v=2$, then $\tau'_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},v}=1$ and also $g_v\ge1$ by the stability of $\Gamma$. Hence
\[
d_v=g_v\le 2g_v-1=k_v-1.
\]

If $\delta_v\ge 4$, then, using quasi-Eulerianity,
\[
d_v\le g_v-1+\left\lceil\frac{\delta_v}{2}\right\rceil
\le 2g_v-3+\delta_v
= k_v-1.
\]

It remains to consider the case $v_i\ne w_i$ and $\delta_v=3$. Then $e_i$ is the unique edge of $S$ incident to $v$, and it is outgoing. By the previous paragraph, exactly one internal incidence of $v$ inside $\Gamma_i$ enters $v$. Hence $\tau'_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},v}=1$, so
\[
d_v=g_v\le 2g_v=k_v-1.
\]

We now prove (iii). Fix $i$, and let us prove the inequality for the edge $e_{i-1}$, whose target is
$w_i=\tau_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(e_{i-1})$. If $v_i=w_i$ and $\delta_{w_i}=2$, then
$\tau'_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},w_i}=1$, so $d_{w_i}=g_{w_i}\ge 1$ by the stability of $\Gamma$. If $\delta_{w_i}\ge 4$, then
$d_{w_i}\ge g_{w_i}-1+\lfloor\delta_{w_i}/2\rfloor\ge 1$. The only remaining case is
$v_i\neq w_i$ and $\delta_{w_i}=3$. Then $e_{i-1}$ is the unique edge in $S$ incident to $w_i$,
and it is incoming; by the previous paragraph, exactly one internal incidence inside $\Gamma_i$ enters $w_i$.
Hence $\tau'_{o,w_i}=2$, so $d_{w_i}=g_{w_i}+1\ge 1$.
This concludes our proof.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:numerical}
    Let $\Gamma$ be a connected stable graph and let $\underline{d}=\underline{d}_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}\in \Sigma(\Gamma)$. Then $0\le d_v\le k_v$ for all $v\in V(\Gamma)$. Moreover, $d_v=0$ (respectively, $d_v=k_v$)
    if and only if $g_v=0$, $t_v=1$, $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=-\delta_v+2$ (respectively, $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=\delta_v-2$). 
    
    If, in addition, $\underline{d}\in \Sigma^{\operatorname{qE}}(\Gamma)$, then $d_v=0$ (respectively, $d_v=k_v$) if and only if $g_v=0$,  $t_v=1$, $\delta_v=3$, $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=-1$ (respectively, $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=1$).
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Recall Equations~\eqref{eq:d-orient}, \eqref{eq:strong}, \eqref{eq:Delta}. The case $|V(\Gamma)|=1$ is immediate;  we assume $|V(\Gamma)|\geq 2$.
Applying Equation~\eqref{eq:strong} to $V=\{v\}$ gives
\begin{equation} \label{eq: ineq-dv}
g_v-1+t_v\le d_v\le g_v-1+\delta_v-t_v.
\end{equation}

If $g_v\ge 1$, then, by the stability of $\Gamma$, we have $g_v-1+t_v>0$. Since
\[
k_v-(g_v-1+\delta_v-t_v)=g_v-1+t_v,
\]
we get $0<d_v<k_v$.

Assume now that $g_v=0$. Then $w_\Gamma(v)=0$, so
$d_v=\tau_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},v}-1$. We have 
\[
\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=\tau_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},v}-\sigma_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},v}
=2\tau_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},v}-\delta_v.
\]
Since $\Gamma$ is connected and stable, $\delta_v\ge 3$ and $t_v\ge 1$; hence \eqref{eq: ineq-dv} gives
\[
0\le d_v\le \delta_v-2=k_v.
\]
Moreover, equality on either side forces $t_v=1$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq: dv=0}
d_v=0
\iff t_v=1,\ \tau_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},v}=1
\iff t_v=1,\ \Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=-\delta_v+2,
\end{equation}
and similarly
\begin{equation} \label{eq: dv=kv}
d_v=k_v
\iff t_v=1,\ \tau_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o},v}=\delta_v-1
\iff t_v=1,\ \Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=\delta_v-2.
\end{equation}




Finally, assume that $\underline{d}\in\Sigma^{\operatorname{qE}}(\Gamma)$. Thus, the chosen
orientation $\operatorname{\mathfrak o}$ satisfies $|\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)|\le 1$. If $d_v=0$, we have seen that $g_v=0$, $t_v=1$ and $|\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)|=\delta_v-2$. Hence, the stability of $\Gamma$ implies $\delta_v=3$ so, by \eqref{eq: dv=0} and \eqref{eq: dv=kv} we have $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=-1$ when $d_v=0$, and $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=1$ when $d_v=k_v$. 



Conversely, if $g_v=0$, $t_v=1$, $\delta_v=3$, and
$\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=-1$, then
$\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=-\delta_v+2$, so \eqref{eq: dv=0} gives $d_v=0$. Similarly, if
$g_v=0$, $t_v=1$, $\delta_v=3$, and $\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=1$, then
$\Delta_{\operatorname{\mathfrak o}}(v)=\delta_v-2$, so \eqref{eq: dv=kv} gives $d_v=k_v$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
(\cite{alexeev}) \label{def: SSAP}
A \emph{stable semi-abelic pair (SSAP)} is a pair $A = (G\operatorname{\curvearrowright} P, \Theta)$ such that 
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(a)] $G$  is a semiabelian variety over $k$.
    \item[(b)] $P$ is a seminormal, connected, projective variety of pure dimension \footnote{We follow \cite[Definition 1.2.4(ii)]{Cap-Viv} in requiring $P$ to be pure dimensional; \cite[Definition 1.1.5]{alexeev} only requires $P$ and $G$ to have the same dimension.} equal to $\dim G$.
    \item[(c)] $G$ acts on $P$ with finitely many orbits, with connected and reduced stabilizers contained in the toric part of $G$.
    \item[(d)] $\Theta$ is an effective ample Cartier divisor on $P$, not containing any $G$-orbit.
\end{itemize}     
We let $P_0$  be the union of the maximal $G$-orbits and we set $\Theta_0 := \Theta\cap P_0$.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:connected-union-ssap}
If $A=(G\operatorname{\curvearrowright} P,\Theta)$ is a SSAP, and $P'\subseteq P$ is a  connected or empty union of irreducible components, then
$A'=(G\operatorname{\curvearrowright} P',\Theta|_{P'})$ is also a SSAP.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{def:GaussA}
    Let $A=(G\operatorname{\curvearrowright} P, \Theta)$ be a SSAP  and consider $\Theta^{\operatorname{sm}}_0=\Theta^{\operatorname{sm}} \cap \Theta_0$. 
The \emph{Gauss map} of $A$ is defined as
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal G\colon \Theta^{\operatorname{sm}}_0 & \to \mathbb{P}(T_0G)^{\vee}\\
         p&\mapsto \mathbb{P}(T_0p^{-1}\Theta).
\end{align*}
(Since $p\in \Theta^{\operatorname{sm}}_0$, we have that $0$ is a smooth point of $p^{-1}(\Theta)$.) The (closure of the) \emph{graph of the Gauss map} of $A$ is defined as
\[
\Upsilon = \Upsilon_A := \overline{\{(p, \mathcal G(p)), p\in \Theta^{\operatorname{sm}}_0\}}\subseteq \Theta\times \mathbb{P}(T_0G)^\vee.
\]
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:SSAPstab}
    If $g_C\geq 2$,  there is a canonical isomorphism $A(C) \to A(C^{\rm{st}})$ of SSAPs (see \cite[Remark~1.3.1]{Cap-Viv}).
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:bijection-irred}
If $C$ has no separating nodes, there is a bijection between the set of stabel multidegree $\Sigma(C)$ and the set of irreducible components of $\overline{P^{g-1}_C}$ mapping each $\underline{d}\in \Sigma(C)$ to $\overline{P_C^{\underline{d}}}$.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:tangent_L_theta}
Let $C$ be a connected nodal curve of genus  $g\geq 2$ with no separating nodes. Let $u=(\emptyset,[I])$ be a general element of an irreducible component of 
$\Theta(C)$. Then
       \[
    T_0 u^{-1}\Theta(C)=\operatorname{Im}(H^0(C,\omega_C\otimes I ^{-1})\otimes H^0(C, I)\to H^0(C, \omega_C))^\perp \subseteq H^0(C, \omega_C)^{\vee}.
    \]
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Since $u$ is general, by \cite[Proposition 3.2.1]{captheta} we have that $h^0(C, I) = 1$, hence $h^0(C, \omega_C\otimes I^{-1})=1$ by Riemann-Roch. The result follows by standard deformation arguments, such as those in \cite[Chapter~3, Section~3.3]{sernesi}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rem:obs-zero-locus}
Let $S$ be a scheme, let $W$ be a finite-dimensional vector space, and let
$e\colon W\otimes\mathcal O_S\to \mathcal E$ be a morphism to a vector bundle $\mathcal E$ on $S$.
Let $Z\subseteq S\times \mathbb P(W)$ be the zero locus of the composition
\[
\pi_2^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(W)}(-1)
\longrightarrow
W\otimes\mathcal O_{S\times \mathbb P(W)}
\longrightarrow
\pi_1^*\mathcal E,
\]
where $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$ are the projections from $S\times \mathbb P(W)$ onto the first and second factor, respectively. 
For $D\in S$, the scheme-theoretic fiber $Z_D$ is naturally identified with
\[
\mathbb P(\ker(e_D))\subseteq \mathbb P(W).
\]

Moreover, if $T\subseteq S$ is an open subset such that
$\mathcal K:=\ker(e|_T)$ is a vector subbundle of $W \otimes \mathcal{O}_T$, then
\[
Z_T=\mathbb P_T(\mathcal K),
\]
where $Z_T$ denotes the inverse image of $T$ in $Z$.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
\label{def: omegad}
Let $C$ be a connected stable curve without separating nodes of genus $g\ge2$. Let $\underline{d}\in \mathbb Z^{V(\Gamma_C)}$ be a multidegree with  degree $|\underline{d}|=g-1$ with $d_v\geq 0$ for all $v$. We define $\widehat{\Omega}_{\underline{d}}\subseteq S_{\underline{d}}(\widehat{C}^\nu)\times \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$ as the zero locus of $\sigma_C$, i.e., we set
\[
\widehat{\Omega}_{\underline{d}}:= Z(\sigma_C) \subseteq S_{\underline{d}}(\widehat{C}^\nu)\times \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C.
\]
Consider the finite map $(\widehat{\varphi}_*,\operatorname{id})\colon S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)\times\operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee\to S_{\underline{d}}(\widehat{C}^\nu)\times \operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee$ (see Equation~\ref{eq:phi-hat-star}). We also define
\[
\Omega_{\underline{d}}:=(\widehat{\varphi}_*, \operatorname{id})^{-1}(\widehat{\Omega}_{\underline{d}})\subseteq S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)\times\operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee.
\]
We call $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ the \emph{Gauss graph of the symmetric product of $C$}.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rem:Omega_d} 
Let $\underline{d}\in \Sigma(C)$. The following properties are easy consequences of the definitions. 
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is non-empty.
    \item[(ii)] We have (recall the notation of Section \ref{sec:schemes}, Diagram \ref{diag:normalizations} and \eqref{eq: defDh} for the definitions of $D_0$ and of $D_h$)
    \[
    \Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1} =\{(D, H) : \ D_0+D_{\operatorname{h}}+\iota_{\operatorname{h}}^*(D_{\operatorname{h}})\leq \nu^*\varphi^*(H)\}\subseteq S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)\times \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1.
    \]
    \item[(iii)] Consider $(D,H)\in \Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}$. Since $2\deg(D|_{C_h^\nu}) = \deg(\nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C_{h}^\nu})$ (by Lemma~\ref{lem:dimdeg}(iv)), we must have  $D_h+\iota_{\operatorname{h}}^*(D_h) = \nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C_{h}^\nu}$. So, if $p\in C_h^\nu$ is a point, then  
    \[
    \mu_p(D) + \mu_{\iota_{\operatorname{h}}(p)}(D) = \mu_{p, H},
    \]
    where $\mu_{p, H} = \mu_p(\nu^*\varphi^*(H))$.   
    In particular, if  $0<\mu_{p,H}\cdot p\le D_{\operatorname{h}}$,
    then we cannot have $\iota^*_{\operatorname{h}}(p)\le D_{\operatorname{h}}$, for otherwise
    \[
    \mu_p(D) + \mu_{\iota_{\operatorname{h}}(p)}(D) \geq \mu_{p, H} + 1.
    \]
     
     \item[(iv)]   
     Given $H\in \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$, let $W_H\subseteq \widehat{C}$ be the maximal subcurve contained in $H$. Let  $Y^\nu_H$ be the complementary subcurve of $\nu^{-1}(\varphi^{-1}(W_H))$ in $C^\nu$. Then 
    \[
    \rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(H)=\{(D,H) :\ (D_0+D_{\operatorname{h}}+\iota_{\operatorname{h}}^*(D_{\operatorname{h}}))|_{Y^\nu_H}\le \nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{Y^\nu_H}\}.
    \]
    (Recall Equation \eqref{eqdef:kappa}). In particular, $\dim(\rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(H))=d_{\varphi^{-1}(W_H)}$ and $\rho_{\underline{d}}$ is dominant.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:Irred_comp}
Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a morphism of schemes with $Y$ irreducible. For every integer $i\ge0$, define 
\[
Y_i=\{y\in Y : \dim f^{-1}(y) = i\}.
\]
Assume that the following properties hold
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] for every irreducible component $X'$ of $X$ we have $\dim X'\ge\dim Y$;
    \item[(ii)] the inequality $\operatorname{codim}_Y Y_i \geq  i +  1$ holds for every $i>0$.
\end{itemize}
Then every irreducible component of $X$ dominates $Y$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let $X'$ be an irreducible component of $X$ that does not dominate $Y$. In particular $\dim f(X') < \dim Y$. By the theorem of the dimension of the fibers, we  have $\dim f(X') + \dim f^{-1}(y) \geq \dim(X') \geq \dim(Y)$ for a general point $y \in f(X')$. Set $i_0 = \dim f^{-1}(y)$. Notice that  $i_0>0$, since $\dim f(X') < \dim Y$ and $\dim(X')\ge \dim (Y)$. We have that $Y_{i_0}\cap f(X')$ is open in $f(X')$. In particular $\dim(Y_{i_0})\geq \dim f(X') \geq \dim(Y) - i_0$, hence $\operatorname{codim}_YY_{i_0}\leq i_0$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:Omega}
Let $C$ be a connected stable curve of genus $g\ge2$ with no separating nodes.
Let $\underline{d}\in\Sigma(C)$.
The following properties hold.
\begin{itemize}

\item[(i)]
   The locus where the dominant map $\rho_{\underline{d}}\colon \Omega_{\underline{d}}\to \operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee$ is finite equals
   \[
   \operatorname{\mathcal U}_{\underline{d}} := \{H\in \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C : \dim(H\cap W)=0, \forall\; W\in \operatorname{Irr}(\widehat{C})
   \text{ with } d_{\varphi^{-1}(W)}>0\}.
   \]
   Notice that $\operatorname{\mathcal U}_{\underline{d}}$ is open and it contains $\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1$ (and hence $\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0$).
\item[(ii)]
   $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is generically smooth, Cohen-Macaulay, integral, and of dimension $g-1$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
First, we claim that each irreducible component of $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ has dimension at least $g-1$. Indeed, by the discussion after Equation \eqref{eq:sigma}, $\widehat\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is the zero locus of a
section of a rank $g-1$ vector bundle on
$S_{\underline{d}}(\widehat C^\nu)\times\mathbb P_C^\vee$. Pulling this section back via
$(\widehat\varphi_*,\mathrm{id})$, we see that $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is the zero locus of a
section of a rank $g-1$ vector bundle on
$S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)\times\mathbb P_C^\vee$. This proves the claim. 

Let us prove (i). By Remark
\ref{rem:Omega_d} (iv), $\rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(H)$ is finite if and only if $H$ contains
no irreducible component $W$ of $\widehat C$ with $d_{\varphi^{-1}(W)}>0$, i.e., if
and only if $H\in \operatorname{\mathcal U}_{\underline{d}}$. Since $\rho_{\underline{d}}$ is proper, this ends the proof of (i).

Let us prove (ii). Set $S_{\underline{d}}:=S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)$, and let $\kappa_{\underline{d}}\colon \Omega_{\underline{d}}\to S_{\underline{d}}$ be the map defined in Equation \eqref{eqdef:kappa}. Let $\mathcal E_{\underline{d}}$ be the pullback to $S_{\underline{d}}$ of
$\widehat{\varphi}^*((\pi_{\underline{d}})_*
( \mathcal O_{\widehat C^\nu}(1)|_{ \widehat{\mathcal D}}))$, and consider the
evaluation map
\begin{equation} \label{eq: evaluation}
e_{\underline{d}}\colon H^0(C,\omega_C)\otimes \mathcal O_{S_{\underline{d}}}\longrightarrow \mathcal E_{\underline{d}}.
\end{equation}
For $D\in S_{\underline{d}}$, taking the fiber over $D$ gives the evaluation map
\[
e_{\underline{d},D}\colon H^0(C,\omega_C)\longrightarrow
H^0(\widehat\varphi_*D,\mathcal O_{\widehat\varphi_*D}(1)).
\]

We define
\[
\mathcal V_{\underline{d}}:=\{D\in S_{\underline{d}}:\operatorname{rk}(e_{\underline{d},D})=g-1\}
=\{D\in S_{\underline{d}}:\dim(\operatorname{span}(\widehat{\varphi}_*(D)))=g-2\}.
\]
This is an open subset of $S_{\underline{d}}$. Since $S_{\underline{d}}$ is a product of symmetric powers of smooth
irreducible curves, $S_{\underline{d}}$ is smooth and irreducible; hence so is $\mathcal V_{\underline{d}}$, if nonempty.

Over $\mathcal V_{\underline{d}}$, the map $e_{\underline{d}}$ is surjective. Set
$\mathcal L:=\ker(e_{\underline{d}}|_{\mathcal V_{\underline{d}}})$. Then $\mathcal L$ is a line bundle, and Remark
\ref{rem:obs-zero-locus} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kappaV}
\kappa_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(\mathcal V_{\underline{d}})=\mathbb P_{\mathcal V_{\underline{d}}}(\mathcal L)\cong \mathcal V_{\underline{d}}.
\end{equation}
Under this isomorphism, a divisor $D\in\mathcal V_{\underline{d}}$ corresponds to the point
$(D,\operatorname{span}(\widehat{\varphi}_*(D)))\in\Omega_{\underline{d}}$. In particular,
$\kappa_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(\mathcal V_{\underline{d}})$ is smooth and irreducible.

We now prove that $\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}$ is irreducible. Let $G\subseteq \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1$ be
a dense open subset such that, for every $H\in G$, the divisor $H\cap\widehat C$
is reduced and Theorem \ref{thm:general_position} applies. The fiber $\rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(H)$ is nonempty for $H\in G$: choose the points
componentwise, using $0\leq d_v\leq k_v$ (see Lemma~\ref{lem:numerical}) on the non-hyperelliptic components
and Lemma~\ref{lem:dimdeg} (ii),(iv) on the honest hyperelliptic components
and pairs.

Let $(D,H)\in \rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(G)$. By Remark \ref{rem:Omega_d} (iii),
Theorem \ref{thm:general_position}, and Lemma \ref{lem:dimdeg} (iii), we have
$\operatorname{span}(\widehat\varphi_*D)=H$. Hence $D\in\mathcal V_{\underline{d}}$, and therefore $\rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(G)\subseteq \kappa_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(\mathcal V_{\underline{d}})$. Since $\rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(G)$ is a nonempty open subset of the irreducible scheme
$\kappa_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(\mathcal V_{\underline{d}})$, it is irreducible. By (i) and the claim at the beginning of the proof, every irreducible component of $\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}$ has dimension
$g-1$ and dominates $\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1$. Hence $\rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(G)$ is dense in
$\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}$. Since $\rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(G)$ is irreducible, so is
$\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}$.

Now we prove that $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is irreducible. For $i\ge0$, set
\[\mathbb P^\vee_{C,i}:=\{H\in \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C:\dim(\rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(H))=i\}.\]
By Remark \ref{rem:Omega_d} (iv), if $i>0$, then
$\mathbb P^\vee_{C,i}$ is contained in the union of the linear spaces $\Lambda_W^\vee$ such that
$d_{\varphi^{-1}(W)}=i$. Hence, using Lemma \ref{lem:dimdeg} (iii),
\[
\dim \mathbb P^\vee_{C,i}\leq
\max_W(\dim(\operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C)-N_W-1)<g-1-i.
\]
Thus $\operatorname{codim}_{\operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee}\mathbb P^\vee_{C,i}\geq i+1$ for every $i>0$.
By the claim at the beginning of the proof and Lemma \ref{lem:Irred_comp}, every irreducible component of
$\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ dominates $\operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee$. Since $\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}$ is irreducible,
there is only one such component. Hence $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is irreducible.

The equality $\dim\Omega_{\underline{d}}=g-1$ follows from (i) and
$\dim(\operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C)=g-1$. Moreover, $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is Cohen-Macaulay by
\cite[Proposition 7.1]{fulton}: it has the expected dimension, it is the zero locus
of a section of a rank $g-1$ vector bundle on the Cohen-Macaulay scheme
$S_{\underline{d}}\times \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$.

Finally, $\kappa_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(\mathcal V_{\underline{d}})\cong \mathcal V_{\underline{d}}$ (see Equation \eqref{eq:kappaV}) is a nonempty smooth open subset of
$\Omega_{\underline{d}}$. Since $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is irreducible, this open subset is dense.
Thus $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is generically smooth, hence generically reduced. Since a
Cohen-Macaulay scheme has no embedded associated points, generically reduced
implies reduced. Therefore $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is reduced. Being irreducible and
reduced, $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is integral.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:rho-branch}
Let $C$ be a connected stable curve of genus $g\ge2$ with no separating nodes. Let $\underline{d}\in \Sigma(C)$. Consider
\[
\mathcal B_{\underline{d}}=\{W\in \operatorname{Irr}_{\ge2}(\widehat{C}) : 0<d_Z<k_Z, \text{ for every } Z\in \operatorname{Irr}_W(C)\}.
\]
The branch locus $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ of the map $\rho_{\underline{d}}\colon \Omega_{\underline{d}}\to \operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee$ is 
    \[
    \operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}}) = \left(\bigcup_{W\in \mathcal B_{\underline{d}}} W^\vee\right) 
    \cup\left(\bigcup_{p\in \mathcal B_{\widehat{C}}}\Lambda_p^\vee\right).
    \]
    Moreover, $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}}) = \operatorname{Br}^1(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ and $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ is the closure of $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0})$ in $\operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Recall that the morphism $\rho_{\underline{d}}$ is finite and dominant on $\operatorname{\mathcal U}_{\underline{d}}\subseteq \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$   (see Proposition~\ref{prop:Omega}~(i)). By Proposition \ref{prop:Omega} (ii), we can compute $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d},\mathcal U_{\underline{d}}})$ using Proposition \ref{prop:branch_fiber_number}.  Also, recall that  $C_v$ is the irreducible component of $C$ corresponding to $v\in V(\Gamma_C)$. Finally, recall Equations~\eqref{eq:decomposition} and \eqref{eq:fg} and the notation  
$\{v',v''\}=f^{-1}(v)$ for every $v\in \widehat{V}^\nu_2$. 

First, we claim that the degree of $\rho_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_{\underline{d}}}$ is given by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:degree}
\deg(\rho_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_{\underline{d}}})=\prod_{v\in V_0} \binom{k_v}{d_v} \prod_{v\in V_1} 2^{d_v} \prod_{v\in \widehat{V}^\nu_2}
\binom{d_{v'}+d_{v''}}{d_{v'}}.
                                                        
\end{equation}
Indeed, the degree of $\rho_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_{\underline{d}}}$ is the number of elements in $\rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(H)$ for a general $H\in \operatorname{\mathcal U}_{\underline{d}}$. By Remark~\ref{rem:Omega_d} (ii), this is the number of divisors $D\in S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)$ such that $D_0+D_h+\iota_{\operatorname{h}}^*(D_{\operatorname{h}})\le \nu^*\varphi^*(H)$. Let us consider this relation over the preimage of each component of $\widehat{C}$. 

If $v\in V_0$, then $\varphi|_{C_v}\colon C_v\to \varphi(C_v)$ is birational and $\nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C_v}$ is a reduced effective divisor of degree $k_v$. We then have to choose a degree $d_v$ divisor $D|_{C_v}\leq \nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C_v}$, which gives the contribution of $\binom{k_v}{d_v}$ to Formula \eqref{eq:degree}.

If $v\in V_1$, then $\varphi|_{C_v}\colon C_v\to \varphi(C_v)$ is a $2:1$ map. By Remark~\ref{rem:Omega_d} (iii), we cannot choose points in $\nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C_v}$ in the same preimage over a point in $H\cap \varphi(C_v)$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:dimdeg}~(ii) and (iv) we have that $d_v = \deg(\varphi(C_v))$, so $H$ cuts $\varphi(C_v)$ in $d_v$ distinct points. For each of these $d_v$ points we have to choose exactly one preimage in $C_v$, which gives the contribution of $2^{d_v}$ to Formula~\eqref{eq:degree}. 

Finally, for $v\in \widehat{V}^\nu_2$, set $W_v:=\varphi(C_{v'}\cup C_{v''})(=\varphi(C_{v'})=\varphi(C_{v''}))$. Then $\varphi|_{C_{v'}\cup C_{v''}} \colon C_{v'}\cup C_{v''}\to W_v$ is a $2:1$ map (it restricts to isomorphisms $C_{v'}\to W_v$ and $C_{v''}\to W_v$), where $C_{v'},C_{v''},W_v$ are smooth rational curves. Again by Remark~\ref{rem:Omega_d} (iii), we cannot choose points in $\nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C_{v'}\cup C_{v''}}$ in the same preimage over a point in $H\cap W_v$. By Lemma \ref{lem:dimdeg} (ii) and (iv), we have $d_{v'}+d_{v''}  = \deg(W_v)$, hence $H$ cuts $W_v$ in $d_{v'}+d_{v''}$ distinct points. Inside the set of preimages of these points in $C_{v'}\cup C_{v''}$ via $\varphi\circ\nu$, we have to choose $d_{v'}$ points in $C_{v'}$ and $d_{v''}$ points in $C_{v''}$, and any two of these points have different images in $W_v$. After choosing the $d_{v'}$ points in $C_{v'}$, we have only one choice for the $d_{v''}$ points in $C_{v''}$, so we get the contribution of $\binom{d_{v'}+d_{v''}}{d_{v'}}$ to Formula~\eqref{eq:degree}. This concludes the proof of the claim.

Next, recall that $W_H\subseteq \widehat{C}$ is defined as the maximal subcurve contained in $H$, for every $H\in \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$ (see Remark \ref{rem:Omega_d} (iv)). We now compute the number of preimages of some fixed $H\in \operatorname{\mathcal U}_{\underline{d}}$ via $\rho_{\underline{d}}$, by taking the product of the following terms.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(a)] If $v\in V(\Gamma_C)$ and $\varphi(C_v)\subseteq W_H$, then $d_v=0$ (recall that $H\in \operatorname{\mathcal U}_{\underline{d}}$), and there is no choice of divisors on $C_v$ to be made. In particular the term corresponding to $v$ is equal to $1 = \binom{k_v}{d_v} = \binom{k_v}{0}$.
    
    \item[(b)] If $v\in V_0$ and $\varphi(C_v)\not\subseteq W_H$, write $\nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C_v} = \sum_{i=1}^k a_ip_i$ with $p_i\neq p_j$ for all $i \neq j$. Then the term is the number of ways to  write
    \[
    \sum_{i=1}^k x_i = d_v, \text{ for } 0\leq x_i\leq a_i.
    \]
    This term is smaller than $\binom{k_v}{d_v}$ if and only if at least one $a_i\geq 2$ and $0 < d_v < k_v$. 
    
    \item[(c)]  If $v \in V_1$ and $\varphi(C_v)\not\subseteq W_H$, write 
    \[
    \nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C_v} = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i(p_i +q_i) + 2\sum_{j=1}^{k'} b_j r_j,
    \]
    where $p_i,q_i$ are pairwise distinct conjugate pairs and $r_j$ are distinct ramification points of the $2:1$ map $C_v\to \varphi(C_v)$. The term is equal to $\prod_{i=1}^{k}(a_i + 1)$, which is strictly smaller than $2^{d_v}$ if and only if $k'\neq 0$ or some $a_i\geq 2$. Notice a special case: if $\varphi(C_v)$ is a line, we never have $a_i \geq 2$.
    
    \item[(d)] If $v\in\widehat{V}^\nu_2$ and $\varphi(C_{v'}\cup C_{v''})\not\subseteq W_H$, write $\nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C_{v'}} = \sum a_ip_i'$. In particular $\nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C_{v''}} = \sum a_ip_i''$, where each $p_i''$ is the image of $p_i'$ via the involution $\iota \colon C_{v'}\to C_{v''}$. Then, we have to choose a divisor $D_{v'}\leq \sum a_ip_i'$ on $C_{v'}$ and this forces the choice of the divisor $D_{v''}=\iota_*(\sum a_ip'_i - D_{v'})$ on $C_{v''}$. This term equals the number of ways to write
    \[
    \sum_{i=1}^k x_i = d_{v'}, \text { for } 0\leq x_i\leq a_i.
    \]
    This term is strictly smaller than $\binom{\sum a_i}{d_{v'}} = \binom{d_{v'}+d_{v''}}{d_{v'}}$ if and only if there is at least one $a_i\geq 2$, and also $d_{v'}>0$ and $d_{v''}>0$. Notice that $d_{v'}+d_{v''}=k_{v'}=k_{v''}$, so we also have $d_{v'}<k_{v'}$ and $d_{v''}<k_{v''}$.
\end{itemize}

Summing up, $H \in\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_{\underline{d}}})$ if and only if either $H$ is tangent to some $W\in \operatorname{Irr}(\widehat{C})$ (and $W\not\subseteq H$) with $0 < d_Z < k_Z$, for every $Z\in \operatorname{Irr}(\varphi^{-1}(W))$, or $H$ contains a point $p\in \mathcal B_{\widehat{C}}$. Since the components of the canonical model of a nodal curve are nodal (as it follows from \cite[Remark~3.8]{catanese}), the first condition is equivalent to $H\in \mathcal \bigcup_{W\in \mathcal B_{\underline{d}}}W^\vee$ by Proposition \ref{prop:dual}. The second condition is equivalent to $H\in \Lambda^\vee_p$, for $p\in \mathcal B_{\widehat{C}}$. This yields the formula for $ \operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ in the statement. In particular, we see that $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})= \operatorname{Br}^1(\rho_{\underline{d}})$. Finally, every irreducible component of $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ intersects $\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0$, hence $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ is the closure of $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0})$. This concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:rho-ramif}
Let $C$ be a connected stable curve of genus $g\ge2$ with no separating nodes. Let $\underline{d}\in \Sigma(C)$. The following properties hold.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] 
      The ramification locus $\operatorname{Ram}(\rho_{\underline{d}}) \subseteq\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ of the map $\rho_{\underline{d}}\colon \Omega_{\underline{d}}\to \operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee$ satisfies 
    \[
     \left(\underset{0<d_v<k_v}{\bigcup_{v\in V(\Gamma_C)}}\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d},v}\right)\cup\left(\underset{\varphi(p)\in\mathcal B_{\widehat{C}}}{\bigcup_{p\in C}} \operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d}, p}\right)\subseteq \operatorname{Ram}(\rho_{\underline{d}}).
    \]
    \item[(ii)] For every $v\in V(\Gamma_C)$ with $0<d_v<k_v$ let   $W_v=\varphi(C_v)$. If $\deg(W_v) >1$ then 
     $\operatorname{codim}_{S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)}(\kappa_{\underline{d}}(\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d},v}))=1$ and $\rho_{\underline{d}}(\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d}, v}) = W_v^{\vee}$.
    \item[(iii)] For every $p\in C$ with $\varphi(p)\in\mathcal B_{\widehat{C}}$, we have $\operatorname{codim}_{S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)}(\kappa_{\underline{d}}(\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d}, p}))=1$ and $\rho_{\underline{d}}(\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d}, p}) = \Lambda_{\varphi(p)}^{\vee}$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
We prove (i). Since $\operatorname{Ram}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ is closed, it suffices to prove the inclusion 
    \[
     \left(\underset{0<d_v<k_v}{\bigcup_{v\in V(\Gamma_C)}}\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d},v}^0\right)\cup\left(\underset{\varphi(p)\in\mathcal B_{\widehat{C}}}{\bigcup_{p\in C}} \operatorname{Ram}^0_{\underline{d}, p}\right)\subseteq \operatorname{Ram}(\rho_{\underline{d}}).
    \]
Since $\mathcal U_1\subseteq\mathcal U_{\underline d}$,
Proposition~\ref{prop:Omega}(i) shows that the restriction
\(
\rho_{\underline d,\mathcal U_1}\colon
\Omega_{\underline d,\mathcal U_1}\to \mathcal U_1
\)
is finite and dominant, with integral Cohen--Macaulay source and smooth target. So we can use  Proposition~\ref{prop:branch_fiber_number}. We shall use that, after
base change along a morphism $\operatorname{Spec}(R)\to\mathcal U_1$ from the spectrum of a DVR, two
distinct points of the generic fiber cannot specialize to the same
unramified point.


We start by proving the inclusion $\operatorname{Ram}^0_{\underline{d}, v} \subseteq \operatorname{Ram}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ for all $v \in V(\Gamma_C)$. Recall the decomposition $V(\Gamma_C) = V_0 \sqcup V_1 \sqcup V_2$ in Equation \eqref{eq:V-decomposition}. In what follows, given a hyperplane $H$ in $\operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee$, we will consider a family $\mathcal H\to \operatorname{Spec}(R)$ of hyperplanes, where $R$ is a DVR, with generic point $\eta$, whose fiber over $\eta$ is equal to a general hyperplane $H_\eta$ and whose fiber over the special point is equal to $H$.

First, fix $v\in V_0$ with $0<d_v<k_v$ and let $(D, H) \in \operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d}, v}^0$. Then there is a point $p_0 \in C^{\operatorname{sm}}\cap C_v$, and an integer $a_0\geq 1$ such that 
\[
\nu^*\varphi^*(H) = (a_0 + 1)p_0 + E,
\]
for some effective divisor $E$ on $C^\nu$, and such that $D = a_0p_0 + D'$, for some $D'$ satisfying $\mu_{p_0}(D') = 0$ (Note that we do not impose that $\mu_{p_0}(E)=0$). Then 
\[
\nu^*\varphi^*(H_\eta) = \sum_{i=1}^{a_0+1}p_{i,\eta} + E_\eta,
\]
where $p_{i,\eta}$ specializes to $p_0$, for every $i=1, \ldots, a_0+1$, and where $E_\eta$ specializes to $E$. For $j=1, \ldots, a_0+1$, we define
\[
D_{j,\eta} := \left(\sum_{i=1}^{a_0+1}p_{i,\eta}\right) - p_{j,\eta} +  D'_\eta,
\]
where $D'_{\eta}$ is any divisor specializing to $D'$ and satisfying (recall Remark \ref{rem:Omega_d} (ii)) 
\[
(D'_{\eta})_0 + (D'_{\eta})_{\operatorname{h}}+ \iota_{\operatorname{h}}^*((D'_{\eta})_{\operatorname{h}}) \leq E_\eta.
\] 
Therefore $(D_{j, \eta}, H_\eta)\in \Omega_{\underline{d}}$ and $(D_{j,\eta}, H_\eta)$ specializes to $(D, H)$ for each $j=1,\ldots, a_0+1$. Since $a_0\geq 1$, at least two points  $(D_{j,\eta}, H_\eta)$ specialize to $(D,H)$, so $(D, H)\in \operatorname{Ram}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$. 

Next fix $v\in V_1\sqcup  V_2$ with $0<d_v<k_v$, let
$(D,H)\in\operatorname{Ram}^0_{\underline{d},v}$, and choose $p_0$ as in Equation~\eqref{eq:Ramv}.  Set $q_0 := \iota_{\operatorname{h}}(p_0)\neq p_0$ (because $p_0\notin \varphi^{-1}(\mathcal{B}_{C})$). Then, by Remark~\ref{rem:Omega_d} (iii), there exists an integer $a_0\geq 1$ such that
\[
\nu^*\varphi^*(H) = (a_0+ 1)(p_0+q_0) + E,
\]
and such that $D = a_0p_0 + q_0 + D'$ with $\mu_{p_0}(D') = 0$. Then 
\[
\nu^*\varphi^*(H_\eta) = \sum_{i=1}^{a_0 + 1}(p_{i,\eta} + q_{i,\eta}) + E_\eta,
\]
where $\iota_{\operatorname{h}}(p_{i, \eta}) = q_{i, \eta}$,  $p_{i,\eta}$ specializes to $p_0$, and $q_{i, \eta}$ specializes to $q_0$, for every $i=1, \ldots, a_0+1$, and where $E_\eta$ specializes to $E$.  For $j=1, \ldots, a_0+1$, we define
\[
D_{j,\eta} := \left(\sum_{i=1}^{a_0+1}p_{i,\eta}\right) - p_{j,\eta} +  q_{j, \eta} + D'_\eta,
\]
where $D'_\eta$ is any divisor specializing to $D'$ and satisfying (recall Remark \ref{rem:Omega_d} (ii))
\[
(D'_{\eta})_0 + (D'_{\eta})_{\operatorname{h}} +\iota_{\operatorname{h}}^*((D'_{\eta})_{\operatorname{h}})\leq E_\eta.
\]
In particular, $(D_{j, \eta}, H_\eta)\in \Omega_{\underline{d}}$ and $(D_{j,\eta}, H_\eta)$ specializes to $(D, H)$ for every $j=1,\ldots, a_0+1$. Since $a_0\geq 1$, at least two points  $(D_{j,\eta}, H_\eta)$ specialize to $(D,H)$, so $(D, H)\in \operatorname{Ram}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$. 

We now show the inclusion $\operatorname{Ram}^0_{\underline{d}, p}\subseteq \operatorname{Ram}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ whenever $\varphi(p)\in \mathcal{B}_{\widehat{C}}$. In this case, given $(D,H)\in \operatorname{Ram}^0_{\underline{d}, p}$, we can write 
\[
\nu^*\varphi^*(H) = 2p + E,
\]
for some effective divisor $E$ on $C^\nu$,
and $D = p + D'$ for some $D'$. Since $(D,H)\in\Omega_{\underline{d}}$, we have
\(
D'_0+D'_{\operatorname{h}}+\iota_{\operatorname{h}}^*(D'_{\operatorname{h}})\leq E
\). The generic hyperplane $H_{\eta}$ now satisfies
\[
\nu^*\varphi^*(H_{\eta}) = p_{\eta} + q_{\eta} + E_{\eta},
\]
where $q_\eta=\iota_{\operatorname{h}}(p_\eta)$ and $p_\eta,q_\eta$ specialize to $p$.
Choose a divisor $D'_\eta$ specializing to $D'$ and satisfying
\[
(D'_{\eta})_0+ (D'_{\eta})_{\operatorname{h}}+\iota_{\operatorname{h}}^*((D'_{\eta})_{\operatorname{h}})\leq E_\eta.
\]
Set $D_{1,\eta} := p_{\eta}+D'_{\eta}$ and $D_{2, \eta} := q_{\eta}+D'_{\eta}$. Both pairs $(D_{1,\eta}, H_{\eta})$, $(D_{2, \eta}, H_{\eta})$ belong to $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ and specialize to $(D, H)$, so $(D, H)\in \operatorname{Ram}(\rho_d)$. This ends the proof of (i).

Before proving (ii) and (iii), notice that $\rho_{\underline{d}}$ is generically \'etale (since it is dominant, generically finite and  $\operatorname{char}(k)=0$). Hence $\operatorname{Ram}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ has positive codimension. By (i) and the
birationality of $\kappa_{\underline{d}}$ (see Equation \eqref{eq:kappaV}), the same is true of the two loci inside $S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)$ in (ii) and (iii). It remains to prove that their codimensions are at most $1$.

We prove (ii). If $g=2$ we have nothing to prove since $\deg W_v=1$ for every $v\in V(\Gamma_C)$. Assume that $g\ge 3$. The fact that $\rho_{\underline{d}}(\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d}, v}) = W_v^{\vee}$, where $W_v=\varphi(C_v)$ is clear. Fix $v\in V(\Gamma_C)$ with $0 < d_v < k_v$ and $\deg(W_v)>1$. Choose $v'$ as follows. If $v\in V_1$, set
$v'=v$. If $v\in V_2$, let $v'$ be the other vertex of the corresponding honest hyperelliptic pair. If $v\in V_0$ and $d_v\geq2$,
set $v'=v$; otherwise choose $v'\neq v$ with $d_{v'}>0$.


Let $\underline{d}'$ be the multidegree obtained from $\underline{d}$ by subtracting $1$ at the entries corresponding to $v$ and $v'$ (so $|\underline{d}'|=g-3$). For a subcurve $Z\subseteq C$, set \[\dot{Z}:=(Z\cap C^{\operatorname{sm}})\setminus \varphi^{-1}(\mathcal B_{\widehat{C}}).\] Define  $F_1\subseteq \dot{C}_v\times S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu)\times \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$ and $F_2\subseteq \dot{C}_v\times \dot{C}_{v'}\times S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu)\times\operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$ as 
\begin{align*}
    F_1 & := \left\{(p, D', H) : \begin{array}{l} \exists q\in \dot{C}_{v'} \text{ such that }(p+q+D',H)\in \Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1},\\ 
    \text{with }1\leq \mu_p(p+q+D') < \mu_p(\nu^*\varphi^*(H))
    \end{array}\right\}; \\ \\
    F_2 & := \left\{(p, q, D', H) : \begin{array}{l} (p+q+D', H)\in \Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}, \text{ with}\\ 1\leq \mu_p(p+q+D') < \mu_p(\nu^*\varphi^*(H))
    \end{array}\right\}.
\end{align*}
We have the following commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
F_1 \ar[d, "\zeta_{1, S}"] & F_2 \ar[l, "{\zeta_{2,1}}"'] \ar[d, "{\zeta_{2, S}}"] \ar[r, "{\zeta_{2, R}}"] & \operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d},v}\ar[d, "\kappa_{\underline{d}}"] \\
\dot{C}_v\times S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu)  & \ar[l, "\eta_S"'] \dot{C_v}\times \dot{C}_{v'}\times S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu) \ar[r, "\pi_S"] & S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
where
\begin{enumerate}
    \item the map $\zeta_{2, 1}$ is the  forgetful map $\zeta_{2, 1}(p, q, D', H) = (p, D', H)$;
    \item the map $\zeta_{2, R}$ is defined by $\zeta_{2, R}(p, q, D', H) = (p+q+D', H)$;
    
\item the map $\zeta_{1, S}$ is the forgetful map $\zeta_{1, S}(p, D', H) = (p, D')$;

\item the map $\zeta_{2,S}$ is the forgetful map $\zeta_{2, S}(p, q, D', H) = (p, q, D')$;

\item the map $\eta_S$ is the projection onto the first and third factor;
\item $\pi_S$ is defined by $\pi_S(p,q,D')=p+q+D'$.
\end{enumerate}
Notice that $\zeta_{2, 1}$                         
is a dominant map.

We claim that $\zeta_{1, S}$ is dominant. By the definition of $F_1$, it is enough to prove that, for a general pair $(p,D')\in \dot{C}_v\times  S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu)$, there is $H\in \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$ such that $2p + D'_0 + D'_{\operatorname{h}}+\iota_{\operatorname{h}}^*(D'_{\operatorname{h}})\leq \nu^*\varphi^*(H)$ and, if $C_v$ is contained in an honest hyperelliptic subcurve of $C$, then $2p +\iota_{\operatorname{h}}^*(2p) + D'_0 + D'_{\operatorname{h}} + \iota_{\operatorname{h}}^*(D'_{\operatorname{h}})\leq \nu^*\varphi^*(H)$. This is equivalent to saying that there is $H\in \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$ tangent to $\widehat{C}$ at $\varphi(\nu(p))$ such that $\varphi(\nu(D'))\subseteq H$.   Since $\deg(D') = g-3$, there is a hyperplane $H\in \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$ containing $\varphi(\nu(D'))$ and the tangent line to $\widehat{C}$ at $\varphi(\nu(p))$. Finally, since $\deg(\nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C_v^{\nu}})=k_v> d_v$ and $\deg(\nu^*\varphi^*(H)|_{C^{\nu}_{v'}})=k_{v'}\geq d_{v'}$, there exists $q\in\dot C_{v'}$ such that
$p+q+D'\leq \nu^*\varphi^*(H)$.
Thus $(p,q,D',H)\in F_1$, proving the claim.

By the claim we get that $\zeta_{1,S}\circ \zeta_{2,1}$ is dominant, which means that $\eta_S\circ \zeta_{2, S}$ is dominant. In particular, $\operatorname{codim}_{C_v\times C_{v'}\times S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu)}(\zeta_{2,S}(F_2)) \leq 1$. Since the map $\pi_S$ is dominant and quasi-finite, we have $\operatorname{codim}_{S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)}(\pi_S(\zeta_{2, S}(F_2))) \leq 1$.
Because the above diagram is commutative, we deduce 
\[
(\pi_S\circ \zeta_{2,S})(F_2) = (\kappa_{\underline{d}}\circ\zeta_{2,R})(F_2)\subseteq \kappa_{\underline{d}}(\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d},v}),
\]
which concludes the proof of (ii).

We prove (iii). The fact that $\rho_{\underline{d}}(\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d}, p}) = \Lambda_{\varphi(p)}^{\vee}$ is again clear. Fix $p\in C$ such that $\varphi(p)\in \mathcal B_{\widehat{C}}$. Let $v\in V(\Gamma_C)$ be such that $p\in C_v$.  Let $\underline{d}'$ be the multidegree obtained from $\underline{d}$ by subtracting $1$ at the entry corresponding to $v$ (so $|\underline{d}'|=g-2$). Define $F\subseteq S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu)\times \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$ as
\[
F := \{(D', H);\ (p + D', H)\in \Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}\}.
\]
Since $\deg(D')= g-2$, for a general $D'$, there always exists a hyperplane containing $\varphi(p)$ and  $\varphi(\nu(D'))$. Hence the following map is dominant
\[
\zeta_S\colon F\to S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu)\times \operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C\to S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu),
\]
where the first map is the natural inclusion and the second is the projection onto the first factor. Also define the map $\zeta_R\colon F\to \operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d},p}$ by $\zeta_R(D',H)=(p+D', H)$. We have the following commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
F \ar[d, "\zeta_S"] \ar[r, "\zeta_R"]  & \operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d},p} \ar[d, "\kappa_{\underline{d}}"] \\
 S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu) \ar[r, "s_p"] & S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
where $s_p\colon S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu)\to S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)$ is defined by $s_p(D')=p + D'$. Because the above diagram is commutative, we have 
\[
(s_p\circ \zeta_S)(F) = (\kappa_{\underline{d}}\circ \zeta_R)(F) \subseteq \kappa_{\underline{d}}(\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d},p}).
\]
Since $\zeta_S$ is dominant, we obtain
\[
\operatorname{codim}_{S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)}(s_p\circ \zeta_S(F)) = \operatorname{codim}_{S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)}(s_p(S_{\underline{d}'}(C^\nu))) = 1,
\]
which concludes the proof of (iii).
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:acgh}
    Consider a smooth non-hyperelliptic curve $C$ of genus $g\geq 3$. Then the canonical map $\varphi \colon C\to\widehat{C} \subseteq \mathbb{P}_C$ is an isomorphism.
    
    Let $H \subseteq \mathbb{P}_C$ be a general tangent hyperplane to $\widehat{C}$, and write $\varphi^*(H) = 2p + q_1 + \dots +q_{2g-4}$. Let $H_t$ be a one-parameter family of hyperplanes limiting to $H$ for $t \to 0$, with $\varphi^*(H_t) = p'_t+p''_t + q_{t,1} + \dots + q_{t,2g-4}$. The number of effective divisors $D_t$ of degree $g-1$ such that $D_t\leq \varphi^*(H_t)$ is $\binom{2g-2}{g-1}$. On the other hand, the number of effective divisors $D$ of degree $g-1$ such that $D\leq\varphi^*(H)$ is $\binom{2g-4}{g-3} + \binom{2g-4}{g-2} + \binom{2g-4}{g-1}$. More precisely, these effective divisors are 
    \[
    2p + \sum_{i\in S_1}q_{i}, \;\;\;\;\;  p+\sum_{i\in S_2}q_{i}, \;\;\;\;\;  \sum_{i\in S_3}q_{i}
    \]
    where $S_1, S_2, S_3\subseteq \{1, \ldots, 2g-4\}$ are any subsets with $|S_1| = g-3$, $|S_2| = g-2$, and $|S_3| = g-1$. It is clear that
   \[
   \lim_{t\to 0}\Bigg(p'_t+\sum_{i\in S_2}q_{t,i}\Bigg) = p +  \sum_{i\in S_2}q_i = \lim_{t\to 0} \Bigg(p''_t+\sum_{i\in S_2}q_{t, i}\Bigg).
   \]
   This means that $(p + \sum_{i\in S_2}q_i, H)$ is a ramification point  for every $S_2\subseteq\{1, \ldots, 2g-4\}$ such that $|S_2|=g-2$, while the points $(2p + \sum_{i\in S_1}q_i, H)$ and $(\sum_{i\in S_3}q_i, H)$ are unramified.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- notation-2: body_md -->
\label{not:partial-normalization}
Let $C$ be a nodal curve. For $S\subseteq C^{\operatorname{sing}}$, let
$C_S\to C$ be the partial normalization at $S$, and let
$\mu_S\colon C^\nu\to C_S$ be the induced map. A divisor $D$ on
$C^\nu$ supported on $\nu^{-1}(C^{\operatorname{sm}})$ will also be regarded,
via $\mu_S$, as a divisor on $C_S$; we write
$\mathcal O_{C_S}(D)$ accordingly.
<!-- end notation-2 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
\label{def:T}
   For each $p\in C^{\operatorname{sing}}$, set $\{p',p''\} := \nu^{-1}(p)$. We let $\mathbb T_{\underline{d}}\subseteq S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)$ be the open subset of divisors $D$ satisfying the following properties
\begin{enumerate}
\item for each $p\in C^{\operatorname{sing}}$, we have $\mu_{p'}(D) + \mu_{p''}(D)\leq 1$.

\item if $S_D\subseteq C^{\operatorname{sing}}$ denotes the set of $p\in C^{\operatorname{sing}}$ such that
$\mu_{p'}(D)+\mu_{p''}(D)=1$, and we set
$D^{\rm sm}:=D\cap \nu^{-1}(C^{\rm sm})$, then
$\mathcal O_{C_{S_D}}(D^{\rm sm})$ is stable on $C_{S_D}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:factorize}
Let $C$ be a connected stable curve of genus $g\ge2$ with no separating nodes. Let $\underline{d}\in \Sigma(C)$. The following properties hold.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] The morphism $\beta_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ factors through $\Upsilon_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$, yielding  a finite birational $\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0$-morphism $\beta_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}\colon \Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}\to \Upsilon_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$.
        \item[(ii)] We have an inclusion $\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}\subseteq \Omega_{\mathbb T_{\underline{d}}}$ and $\beta_{\mathbb T_{\underline{d}}}|_{\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}} = \beta_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$.
        \item[(iii)] The morphism $\beta _{\mathbb T_{\underline{d}}}$ factors through $\Upsilon_{\underline{d}}$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Let $V\subseteq \Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ be the open subset consisting of pairs $(D,H)$
such that $h^0(C,\mathcal O_C(D))=1$. The general element of
$\Theta_{\underline{d}}$ has exactly one section by \cite[Proposition 3.2.1]{captheta};
hence $V$ is dense in $\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$.

Take $(D,H)\in V$ and set $I:=\mathcal O_C(D)$. Let
$\ell_H\subseteq H^0(C,\omega_C)$ be the line  corresponding to
$H\in\mathbb P_C^\vee$. Since $(D,H)\in\Omega_{d,\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$, the sections in
$\ell_H$ vanish along $\nu(D)$; hence
\[
\ell_H\subseteq
H^0(C,\omega_C\otimes I^{-1})
=
H^0(C,\omega_C(-D)).
\]
Since $h^0(C,I)=1$, Riemann--Roch gives
$h^0(C,\omega_C\otimes I^{-1})=1$. Therefore
\[
H=
\mathbb P\bigl(H^0(C,\omega_C\otimes I^{-1})\bigr)
=
\mathbb P\bigl(H^0(C,\omega_C(-D))\bigr)
\in \mathbb P_C^\vee.
\]
Equivalently, the hyperplane of
$\mathbb P_C=\mathbb P(H^0(C,\omega_C)^\vee)$ corresponding to $H$ is
\[
\mathbb P\bigl(H^0(C,\omega_C(-D))^\perp\bigr)\subseteq \mathbb P_C.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent_L_theta}, this hyperplane is $\mathbb P(T_0u^{-1}\Theta(C))$, where $u=[I]$, so $([I],H)\in\Upsilon_{d,\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$. Hence, since $V$ is dense in $\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$, the morphism $\beta_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ factors through $\Upsilon_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$. 

 As noted at the beginning of the proof, the general element of $\Theta_{\underline{d}}$ has only one section, hence the morphism $\beta_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ is birational. We prove that $\beta_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ is finite by showing it is proper and quasi-finite. Since $\gamma_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ and $\rho_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ are proper, $\beta_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ is also proper. Moreover, $\beta_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ is quasi-finite, because it is a $\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0$-morphism, so every fiber of $\beta_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ is contained in a fiber of $\rho_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$, and the latter is finite by  Proposition~\ref{prop:Omega}(i). This ends the proof of (i).

Notice that $\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}\subseteq \Omega_{\mathbb{T}_{\underline{d}}}$. Indeed, if
$(D,H)\in\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$, then $\operatorname{supp}(D)\subseteq\nu^{-1}(C^{\rm sm})$, so
$S_D=\emptyset$ and $\mathcal O_C(D)$ has multidegree $\underline{d}\in\Sigma(C)$. Hence $D\in \mathbb{T}_{\underline{d}}$. Moreover, by Equations \eqref{eq:betaU0_def} and \eqref{eq:beta_def}, we have
$\beta_{\mathbb{T}_{\underline{d}}}(D,H)=\beta_{d,U_0}(D,H)$. This proves (ii).

To prove (iii), it is enough to notice that $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ is irreducible, so the image of $\beta_{\mathbb T_{\underline{d}}}$ lies in the closure of the image of $\beta_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$, which is contained in $\Upsilon_{\underline{d}}$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:equal}
    Let $C$ be a connected stable curve of genus $g\ge2$ with no separating nodes. Let $\underline{d}\in \Sigma(C)$. Then $\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})=\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ (see Equation \eqref{eqdef:kappa}).
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
The proof of the inclusion $\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})\subseteq\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ relies on the following

{\bf Claim:} There exists an open subset $\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger \subseteq \mathbb{P}^{\vee}_C$                        
 such that:
\begin{enumerate}
   \item[(1)] The inequality $\operatorname{codim}_{\operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C}(\operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C\setminus \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger)\geq 2$ holds.
   \item[(2)] The rational map $\beta_{\underline{d}}$ in Lemma \ref{lem:factorize} restricts to a well-defined $\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger$-morphism $\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}\to \Upsilon_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}$ that, by abusing notation, we still call  $\beta_{\underline{d}}$.
   \item[(3)] The morphism $\beta_{\underline{d}}\colon\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}\to \Upsilon_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}$ is finite birational. 
   \item[(4)] The scheme $\widehat{\Upsilon}_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}$ is smooth.
\end{enumerate}


Let us first prove the claim. By Lemma \ref{lem:factorize} (i) we have a rational map $\beta_{\underline{d}}\colon\Omega_{\underline{d}}\dasharrow\Upsilon_{\underline{d}}$ such that $\beta_{\underline{d}}$ restricts to the morphism $\beta_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ defined in Equation \eqref{eq:betaU0_def} over $\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$. Let $\mathcal{D}_{\underline{d}}\subseteq\Omega_{\underline{d}}$ be the open subset where $\beta_{\underline{d}}$ is a morphism, so $\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}\subseteq \mathcal{D}_{\underline{d}}$. 

Recall the definition of the open subset $\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1\subset \operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee$ from Section~\ref{sec:gauss-graph}. Also recall that we have an  inclusion $\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0 \subseteq \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1$, and that the morphism  $\rho_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}\colon \Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}\to \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1$ is finite and dominant (by Proposition~\ref{prop:Omega}(i)). Then define 
\begin{align*}
\mathcal Y &:= \left(\bigcup_{W\in \operatorname{Irr}_{\geq2}(\widehat{C})} W^\vee\right)\cup \left(\bigcup_{p\in \mathcal{B}_{\widehat{C}}} \Lambda^\vee_{p}\right),\\
\operatorname{\mathcal U}' &:= \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0\cup (\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1\setminus \mathcal Y),\\
\mathcal F&:= \Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}'}\setminus \Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}.
\end{align*}



First, $\operatorname{\mathcal U}'$ is an open subset of $\operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C$ with $\operatorname{\mathcal U}'\subseteq\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1$. 
                                                                                 
Also, $\operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^{\vee}\setminus \mathcal U_0 = \bigcup_{p\in \mathcal{S}_{\widehat{C}}}\Lambda_p^\vee$ and $(\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1\setminus \mathcal{Y})\cap \Lambda_p^{\vee} \neq \emptyset$ for every $p\in \mathcal{S}_{\widehat{C}}$, therefore $\operatorname{codim}_{\operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C}(\operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C\setminus\operatorname{\mathcal U}') \geq 2$.

Second, $\mathcal{F}$ is pure of dimension $g-2$. Indeed, this follows from the fact that  $\rho_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}'}\colon \Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}'}\to \operatorname{\mathcal U}'$ is finite and dominant, that $\mathcal F=\rho_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}'}^{-1}(\operatorname{\mathcal U}'\setminus \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0)$, and that 
\[
\operatorname{\mathcal U}'\setminus \operatorname{\mathcal U}_0 = \bigcup_{p \in \mathcal{S}_{\widehat{C}}}(\Lambda_p^\vee \cap (\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1\setminus \mathcal{Y}))
\]
is pure of dimension $g-2$. Moreover, since $\operatorname{\mathcal U}'\subseteq \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1$, we have that $\mathcal F\subseteq \Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}$.

Denote by $\Omega_{\underline{d}}^{\operatorname{sm}}$ the smooth locus of $\Omega_{\underline{d}}$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:branch_fiber_number},
$\rho_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}^1}$ is flat. By Proposition~\ref{prop:rho-branch},
it is unramified along $\mathcal F$, hence étale along $\mathcal F$. Since $\operatorname{\mathcal U}^1$
is smooth, we have $\mathcal F\subseteq\Omega_{\underline{d}}^{\rm sm}$.
Because the indeterminacy locus of a rational map on a smooth source has codimension at least two, we have $\operatorname{codim}_{\Omega_{\underline{d}}^{\operatorname{sm}}}(\Omega_{\underline{d}}^{\operatorname{sm}}\setminus \mathcal{D}_{\underline{d}}) \geq 2$. Thus every irreducible component of $\mathcal F$ has non-empty intersection with $\mathcal{D}_{\underline{d}}$, so $\operatorname{codim}_{\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}'}}(\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}'}\setminus \mathcal{D}_{\underline{d}})\geq 2$. Since $\rho_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}'}\colon\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}'}\to \operatorname{\mathcal U}'$ is finite and dominant, we deduce that  $\operatorname{codim}_{\operatorname{\mathcal U}'}(\rho_{\underline{d}}(\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}'}\setminus \mathcal{D}_{\underline{d}})) \geq 2$. 

We now define the open set $\operatorname{\mathcal U}'' := \operatorname{\mathcal U}'\setminus \rho_{\underline{d}}(\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}'}\setminus \mathcal{D}_{\underline{d}})$. Because  $\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}''}$ is a subset of $\mathcal{D}_{\underline{d}}$, the rational map $\beta_{\underline{d}}$ is a well-defined morphism $\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}''}\to \Upsilon_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}''}$. 
                                                                      
It is clear that $\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}''}\to \Upsilon_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}''}$ is finite

and by Lemma \ref{lem:factorize} (i) it is also birational. Finally, set $\operatorname{\mathcal U}^{\dagger} := \operatorname{\mathcal U}''\setminus \widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}}(\widehat{\Upsilon}^{\operatorname{sing}}_{\underline{d}})$. Since $\widehat{\Upsilon}_{\underline{d}}$ is normal, we have that $\dim \widehat{\Upsilon}^{\operatorname{sing}}_{\underline{d}} \leq g-3$, hence $\dim (\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}}(\widehat{\Upsilon}^{\operatorname{sing}}_{\underline{d}})) \leq g-3$ and therefore $\operatorname{codim}_{\operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^{\vee}}(\operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^{\vee}\setminus \operatorname{\mathcal U}^{\dagger})\geq 2$. The latter statement proves that Item (1) holds, and since we are removing the image of the singular locus, it is clear that Item (4) holds. Items (2) and (3) follow from the fact that $\operatorname{\mathcal U}^{\dagger}\subseteq \operatorname{\mathcal U}''$ and they hold for $\operatorname{\mathcal U}''$. This concludes the proof of the Claim. 

 

We now prove the inclusion $\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})\subseteq \operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:purity} and Proposition~\ref{prop:rho-branch}, both $\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})$ and $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ are pure of codimension~$1$. Hence, by Item~(1) of the Claim, it is enough to prove the inclusion after restricting to $\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger$, since $\mathbb{P}_C^\vee\setminus \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger$ has codimension at least $2$. By Items~(2) and (3) of the Claim and the universal property of the normalization, there is a finite birational morphism $\Psi\colon \widehat{\Upsilon}_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}\to \Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}$; hence $\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d},U^\dagger}
=\rho_{\underline{d},U^\dagger}\circ\Psi$ is finite and dominant, and
$\deg(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})=\deg(\rho_{\underline{d}})$. Now let $H\in \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger\setminus \operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$. Since $\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}$ is Cohen--Macaulay by Proposition~\ref{prop:Omega}~(ii), and since $\mathbb{P}_C^\vee$ is smooth, Proposition~\ref{prop:branch_fiber_number} applied to $\rho_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}$ gives $|\rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(H)|=\deg(\rho_{\underline{d}})$. Moreover, $\Psi$ is surjective on fibers, so $|\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(H)|\ge |\rho_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(H)|$. On the other hand, by Item~(4) of the Claim, $\widehat{\Upsilon}_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}$ is smooth, hence Cohen--Macaulay, and therefore Proposition~\ref{prop:branch_fiber_number} also applies to $\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}$, yielding $|\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(H)|\le \deg(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})$. Since $\deg(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})=\deg(\rho_{\underline{d}})$, we conclude that $|\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(H)|=\deg(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})$, and thus $H\notin \operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})$. This proves the inclusion of branch loci over $\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger$, and hence globally.



We now prove the opposite inclusion
$\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})\supseteq \operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$.
By the last assertion of Proposition~\ref{prop:rho-branch},
$\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d}})$ is the closure of $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0})$ in
$\operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee$. Since $\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})$ contains the
closure of $\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0})$, it is enough to prove the inclusion $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0})
\subseteq
\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0})$.



Recall the evaluation map $e_{\underline{d}}$ from Equation~\eqref{eq: evaluation}, and the open subset
\[
\mathcal V_{\underline{d}}:=\{D\in S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu):  \operatorname{rk}(e_{\underline{d},D})=g-1\} \subseteq  S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu) \] introduced in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:Omega}, and set
\[S_{\underline{d},0}:=\kappa_{\underline{d}}(\Omega_{\underline{d},U_0}),\qquad
\mathcal V_{\underline{d},0}:=\mathcal V_{\underline{d}}\cap S_{\underline{d},0}.
\]
By the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:Omega}(ii),
$\kappa_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(\mathcal V_{\underline{d},0})\cong\mathcal V_{\underline{d},0}$ is a nonempty smooth
open subset of $\Omega_{\underline{d},U_0}$.

Set $S_{\underline{d},0}^1:=S_{\underline{d},0}\setminus\mathcal V_{\underline{d},0}$.
Its inverse image in $\Omega_{\underline{d},U_0}$ is a proper closed subset,
hence has dimension at most $g-2$. Since every fiber over
$S_{\underline{d},0}^1$ has positive dimension, $\dim S_{\underline{d},0}^1\leq g-3$.
As $\dim S_{\underline{d},0}=g-1$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cod2}
\operatorname{codim}_{S_{\underline{d},0}}S_{\underline{d},0}^1\geq2.
\end{equation}

By
Lemma~\ref{lem:factorize}(i) and the universal property of the
normalization, there is a finite birational morphism
\[
\Psi_0\colon
\widehat{\Upsilon}_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}
\longrightarrow
\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}.
\]
Since $\kappa_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(\mathcal V_{\underline{d},0})$ is smooth, and hence normal,
$\Psi_0$ restricts to an isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{eq:phi-restriction}
\Psi_0^{-1}\bigl(\kappa_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(\mathcal V_{\underline{d}, 0})\bigr)
\stackrel{\cong}{\longrightarrow}
\kappa_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(\mathcal V_{\underline{d},0}).
\end{equation}

Now let $v\in V(\Gamma_C)$ be such that $0<d_v<k_v$ and $W=\varphi(C_v)$ has degree at least $2$, and let $p\in C$ be such that $\varphi(p)\in\mathcal B_{\widehat{C}}$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:rho-ramif}(ii) and (iii), we may choose irreducible components $R_v\subseteq\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d},v}$ and $R_p\subseteq\operatorname{Ram}_{\underline{d},p}$ whose images under $\kappa_{\underline{d}}$ have codimension $1$ in $S_{\underline{d}}(C^\nu)$. Since $\rho_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_1}$ is finite, these components dominate $W^\vee$ and $\Lambda_{\varphi(p)}^\vee$, respectively. Hence their intersections with $\Omega_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$ are dense, and Equation~\eqref{eq:cod2} implies that $R_v\cap\kappa_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(\mathcal V_{\underline{d}, 0})$ and $R_p\cap\kappa_{\underline{d}}^{-1}(\mathcal V_{\underline{d}, 0})$ are nonempty, and thus dense in $R_v$ and $R_p$.

By Proposition~\ref{prop:rho-ramif}(i) and Equation~\eqref{eq:phi-restriction}, their inverse images under $\Psi_0$ are contained in the ramification locus of $\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0}$. Their images are dense in $W^\vee\cap\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0$ and $\Lambda_{\varphi(p)}^\vee\cap\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0$, respectively; since the branch locus is closed in $\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0$, we obtain the inclusions $W^\vee\cap\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0\subseteq\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0})$ and $\Lambda_{\varphi(p)}^\vee\cap\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0\subseteq\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0})$. As $v$ and $p$ vary, Proposition~\ref{prop:rho-branch} gives $\operatorname{Br}(\rho_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0})\subseteq\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d},\operatorname{\mathcal U}_0})$, concluding the proof.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
There exists an open subset $\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger \subseteq \mathbb{P}^{\vee}_C$                        
 such that:
\begin{enumerate}
   \item[(1)] The inequality $\operatorname{codim}_{\operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C}(\operatorname{\mathbb P}^\vee_C\setminus \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger)\geq 2$ holds.
   \item[(2)] The rational map $\beta_{\underline{d}}$ in Lemma \ref{lem:factorize} restricts to a well-defined $\operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger$-morphism $\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}\to \Upsilon_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}$ that, by abusing notation, we still call  $\beta_{\underline{d}}$.
   \item[(3)] The morphism $\beta_{\underline{d}}\colon\Omega_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}\to \Upsilon_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}$ is finite birational. 
   \item[(4)] The scheme $\widehat{\Upsilon}_{\underline{d}, \operatorname{\mathcal U}^\dagger}$ is smooth.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:branch-gamma}
     Let $C$ be a connected nodal curve of genus $g\ge2$ with no separating nodes. Let $\underline{d}\in\Sigma(C)$. The branch locus $\operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})$ of the map $\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}}\colon \widehat{\Upsilon}_{\underline{d}}\to \operatorname{\mathbb P}_C^\vee$ is 
    \[
    \operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}}) = \left(\bigcup_{W\in \mathcal B_{\underline{d}}} W^\vee\right) 
    \cup\left(\bigcup_{p\in \mathcal B_{\widehat{C}}}\Lambda_p^\vee\right),
    \]
    where
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:Bd}
\mathcal B_{\underline{d}}=\{W\in \operatorname{Irr}_{\ge2}(\widehat{C}) : 0<d_Z<k_Z, \text{ for every } Z\in \operatorname{Irr}_W(C)\}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, if $\underline{d}\in\Sigma^{\operatorname{qE}}(C)$, then 
\[    \operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma}_{\underline{d}})= \operatorname{Br}(\widehat{\gamma})=\left(\bigcup_{W\in \operatorname{Irr}_{\ge2}(\widehat{C})} 
    W^\vee \right)\cup\left(\bigcup_{p\in\mathcal B_{\widehat C}}\Lambda_p^\vee\right).
    \]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
We can assume that $C$ is stable. Indeed, $A(C)$ is naturally isomorphic to $A(C^{\operatorname{st}})$, the set $\Sigma(C)$ is naturally identified with $\Sigma(C^{\operatorname{st}})$, we have a natural isomorphism $\widehat{C}\cong \widehat{C}^{\operatorname{st}}$, and $\mathcal{B}_{\widehat{C}}=\mathcal{B}_{\widehat{C}^{\operatorname{st}}}$. Moreover, under these identifications, $\operatorname{Irr}_W(C)$ is naturally
identified with $\operatorname{Irr}_W(C^{\rm st})$ for every
$W\in\operatorname{Irr}(\widehat C)$. The first part follows immediately from Propositions \ref{prop:rho-branch} and \ref{prop:equal}.
     
     Next, by Lemma \ref{lem:linear-classification}, for $Z\in \operatorname{Irr}(C)$ with $g_Z=0$ and $\delta_Z=3$ we find that $\varphi(Z)$ is a linear component of $\widehat{C}$. Hence, according to Lemma \ref{lem:numerical},
